# R&D — Genre & perspective hand-off, and the Interlude system

*Written 2026-08-20 for T-0041. Grounded in a three-way code sweep of `D:\UNITY\Laubrary Dev` and `D:\UNITY\OutBurner`; every load-bearing claim below carries a `file:line`. Supersedes parts of `INTERLUDE_DESIGN.md` — see §10.*

---

## 1. What this answers

Two heavy features were put on the table together, and they are related but **not the same problem**:

- **(A) The genre + perspective hand-off.** *"3D racing. Car stops. 90° slide turn into a side pose. Driver gets out, walks right. Screen scrolls right. Platforms and buildings revealed. Game is now a side-scrolling run-and-gun."*
- **(B) Interlude.** A cutscene system that takes control of live agents for stage intros, midboss reveals, stage-clear outros, authored over Cartographer levels.

And one direct question, which §4.1 answers with a recommendation against: *"the transition from 3D to 2D could be solved by imposing a 2D level on the 3D?"*

The short version of everything below: **(A) and (B) share one mechanism and one mechanism only — screen space.** Interlude is the thing that *performs* the hand-off; the hand-off itself is a Cabinet swap, not a level-geometry problem. Treating them as one system would be a mistake; treating them as unrelated would mean building the transition twice.

---

## 2. Ground truth — what already exists, and what genuinely doesn't

Two findings reframe everything below.

**First: `INTERLUDE_DESIGN.md` has no awareness of `Cabinets`** — zero mentions — even though Cabinets is the system that owns projection, virtual resolution and "what gameplay style is on screen". Every conclusion the doc reaches about backdrops, framing and the 3D hand-off was reached without it. (Its treatment of `Arena` is fine, for the avoidance of doubt: `INTERLUDE_DESIGN.md:21` already frames the trio as *"Cartographer = space. **Arena = systemic time.** Interlude = authored time."*)

**Second, and less comfortable: `Arena` has no live consumer in this repo.** Its GUID appears in zero scenes, prefabs or assets in Laubrary Dev; the only place it is actually wired anywhere is OutBurner, at `ScavengeGame.cs:838`. So Arena is well-designed, well-documented, unit-testable — and **unexercised here**. Treat it as a strong foundation that still needs its first local proof, not as a finished road.

### Already built and load-bearing

| Thing | Where | Why it matters here |
|---|---|---|
| **`Cabinet`** — "THE presentation contract for one gameplay style — the arcade cabinet you walk up to" | `Runtime/Cabinets/Cabinet.cs:5` | Holds `virtualResolution` (`:57`), `referencePpu` (`:62`), `Projection {Orthographic, Perspective}`, `WindowFit`. **`Projection.Perspective` is documented verbatim as "Fake-3D / real-3D — the pseudo-racer"** (`Cabinet.cs:32`). The genre switch's data primitive already exists. |
| **`CabinetStage`** | `Runtime/Cabinets/CabinetStage.cs` | `[ExecuteAlways]`; pushes a Cabinet onto a real `Camera` (`orthographicSize` or `fieldOfView`), drives URP `PixelPerfectCamera` by reflection (`:92-145`). |
| **`Arena`** — "where a scene's play happens — **whatever its size, shape or genre**" | `Runtime/Cartographer/Arena.cs:5` | Room lifecycle: `Play()`, `Stop()`, `CurrentRoomIndex`, `ViewCenter`, `RoomStarted`/`LevelFinished`/`PlayerCaught`, and the game-supplied `Func<bool> RoomCleared` (`:43`, consumed `:244`). Crucially it is a **pure `Tick(dt, playerPos)`** (public, `:112`) exposed *"so it can be driven from a test or a cutscene exactly as Update drives it"* (`:15`). Interlude's runtime seam is pre-drilled — but see the "no live consumer" caveat above. |
| **Actor possession primitives** | `Runtime/Zoetrope/MotionState.cs:122`, `Runtime/Zoetrope/AnimationArbiter.cs:13-15` | `MotionStateSource.PublishOverride(MotionState, float)` publishes a motion state that nothing inferred from an actual transform delta. `AnimationArbiter` is a priority claim system built to replace a hardcoded locomotion-vs-reaction special case, so *"a dash, a jump or an aim pose"* had somewhere to plug in — a cutscene is a natural additional claimant, though the code does not name one. |
| **`ChoreographyPlayer`** | `Runtime/Choreographer/ChoreographyPlayer.cs:52-57` | Already drives a `List<Transform>` along an authored path every Update. Scripted actor movement is not new code. |
| **`PathCache`** | `Runtime/Choreographer/ChoreographySampler.cs:168-200` | Catmull-Rom, arc-length paced, takes a bare `List<Vector2>`. Reusable as Interlude's path evaluator without touching Choreographer. |
| **`TextSplash` / `SplashPlayer`** | `Runtime/TextSplash/SplashPlayer.cs:8-17,44-49` | Genuinely runtime, not editor-only — the asmdef has no `includePlatforms` and the one `using UnityEditor` is `#if UNITY_EDITOR`-guarded. Spawns Canvas + TMP, entrance→hold→exit, returns a `SplashHandle` exposing `IsDone`, `IsCancelled`, a `Completed` event and `Cancel()` (not `await`-able in the C# sense). **"STAGE 1 — GET READY" is already shippable today.** |
| **Level→sequence resolver** | `LevelInstance.cs:160-167`, `CartographerRoom.cs:105,113,120` | `TryGetSpot(name, out worldPos)` + `SpotNames`; `reservedAreas` + `IsReserved`; `railPath`. All three things a sequence needs from a level are in the schema already. |
| **`LevelCollision.SideScroll`** | `LevelAsset.cs:111` | The level schema's default collision mode is *already* side-scroll. Cartographer is not a top-down-only tool. |

### Genuinely missing

| Gap | Evidence | Size |
|---|---|---|
| **Any Cabinet-to-Cabinet transition** | Cabinet/CabinetStage set a camera's state; nothing animates *between* two Cabinets. | Small–medium, new |
| **Any runtime 3D→sprite path** | `ShapeForm.Playback3D` is an editor-only POC; `PyrePlusRenderer.cs:634` returns unconditionally for it in the render path (bake included, not merely runtime-gated); all `PreviewRenderUtility` use is Editor-assembly. | Not needed if §4.4 is taken |
| **A 3D `ICharacterView`** | `ICharacterView.Build(GameObject)` (`Runtime/Zoetrope/ICharacterView.cs`) has only 2D implementors (`SpriteView`, `LauminaryView`, `ZonedLauminaryView`, `CompositeLauminaryView`). | Small, and the seam is clean |
| **A possession/suppress flag on the player driver** | `Runtime/ZoeCharacter/TopDownMotionDriver.cs` reads `IZoeInputSource` and moves the body; it has no "someone else owns me now" mode. | Small, but touches the player |
| **Any track/timeline UI control** | Nothing in ZUI's 43 toolkit files. `ZuiStepSequencer` is a *value* painter (N bars, drag to set levels); `ZuiScrub` is a numeric drag helper. The **closest real precedent is PyrePlus CherryFraming** — `CherryFrame.cs` is a slot in an ordered sub-sequence with a per-slot `lengthMultiplier` in beats, and `Editor/PyrePlus/PyrePlusWindow.CherryFraming.cs` is a drag-reorderable slot strip with per-slot duration. Single-track, but the gesture work is done once already. | **Medium–large, the single biggest build item** |
| **A coordinate-space tag on paths** | `Choreography.cs:17-18` documents `pathPoints` as "normalised space" in a comment; no enum, no world/spot/screen distinction. | Small |
| **A hand-off `RoomExit` case** | The enum is `Distance`/`Time`/`ClearEnemies` only — declared at `CartographerRoom.cs:7-15` (not in `Arena.cs`, which only switches on it at `:184-192` and `:240-246`). Parked as OutBurner `TASKS.md:135`. | Trivial |
| **Interlude, at all** | No implementation in either repo. In code it is exactly two things: a `Prop.cs:24` docstring and design notes at `Runtime/Cartographer/TODO.md:186-195`. (Prose mentions in `INTERLUDE_DESIGN.md` and task files aside.) | The subject of §5 |

---

## 3. The thesis: this is three separable problems

Splitting them is what makes the whole thing tractable, and each has a different owner and a different risk profile.

1. **Presentation hand-off** — how does the *picture* change from a 3D perspective racer to a 2D orthographic side-scroller without a cut? Owned by **Cabinets**. Low risk, well-scoped, no dependency on Interlude.
2. **Authority hand-off** — who is driving the player's body, and how does control pass from racer physics → scripted walk → platformer input? Owned by **Interlude + the driver-possession flag**. Medium risk.
3. **Content hand-off** — where does the side-scrolling level come from and how is it authored? Owned by **Cartographer/Arena**, which are *designed* for exactly this and default to side-scroll collision. Lowest design risk of the three, but not zero build risk: Arena has never been run in this repo (§2), so its first job here is to be proven, not merely adopted.

The reason the feature *feels* enormous is that all three fire in the same two seconds. They do not have to be built, or even designed, together.

---

## 4. Problem A — the genre & perspective hand-off

### 4.1 Answer to "impose a 2D level on the 3D?" — recommend **no**

The instinct is understandable but it fuses the two coordinate systems, and that exact fusion has already been ruled against once in this codebase, for the same reason. OutBurner `TASKS.md:200`, decided 2026-07-30: *"`DepthSpace` stops at the pseudo-3D family — do not stretch it to flat 2D genres… **Share the tech stack, not the coordinate system**… A side-scroller has no depth axis at all, and implementing `IDepthSpace` for it would make `play.y` mean depth in a scene whose vertical axis is height — **the naming would lie to whoever authored it.**"*

That ruling applies here verbatim. The racer is genuinely real 3D — `DESIGN.md:9-10` locks it (*"The world exists in real Unity 3D space"*), and `ChaseCamera.cs:56-59` actively warns at runtime if the camera is orthographic. A Cartographer level, by contrast, is a flat cell grid (`LevelAsset.bounds` is a bare `RectInt`, `LevelAsset.cs:107`) with `actorSortingOrder` standing in for depth (`:122`) — there is no Z coordinate anywhere in the schema.

And here is the sharpest form of the argument: **the grid's axes have no fixed meaning, and the project already exploits that.** OutBurner's parked depth-shooter work reads grid Y as *depth*, while a side-scroller reads grid Y as *height*. The same schema, two incompatible interpretations — which is fine precisely because each level is only ever read by one genre at a time. Impose that grid on the 3D racing world and you must pick one interpretation globally and make it agree with real metres. Every authored cell then acquires a meaningless third coordinate, every road metre acquires a meaningless cell index, and the level editor has to show you a 3D world it cannot represent.

**What must be continuous is not the world. It is the screen.**

### 4.2 The Handover Frame — screen space is the lingua franca

At the swap instant, the player is looking at a rectangle of pixels. If the *last frame the 3D camera renders* and the *first frame the 2D camera renders* agree about where the driver is, how big he is, and what is behind him, the cut is invisible — regardless of the two worlds being kilometres apart in Unity coordinates.

This is buildable precisely because **`Cabinet` already makes screen space a shared, first-class quantity**: both cabinets declare a `virtualResolution` (`Cabinet.cs:57`) and a `referencePpu` (`:62`), so "the driver stands at 38% across, 61% down, occupying 22 virtual pixels of height" is a statement both modes can honour. It is also the same idea `INTERLUDE_DESIGN.md` §4 already reached from the other direction, when it concluded a path must declare its coordinate space and that **screen** space is the one portable to *everything*.

So the deliverable is a **Handover Frame**: an authored agreement, stored once, of the screen-space position and scale of the handed-over actor(s), plus the backdrop's screen-space alignment. The 3D side drives its camera until the driver lands on that mark; the 2D side opens with him already on it.

> **Design consequence worth locking early:** the 90° slide turn into a "side pose" in the original description is not decoration — it is **the alignment move**. It exists to rotate the car until its 3D silhouette matches what a side-on sprite will look like, so the swap has something to match. Keep it. It is the cheapest possible solution to the hardest part of the problem, and it was arrived at intuitively.

### 4.3 The mechanism: `CabinetTransition`

New, small, and the highest-value single piece of work in this document.

- Take two Cabinets and a duration; drive the visible camera state from one to the other.
- **Recommended technique: dual-camera cross-dissolve via RenderTexture.** Both cameras render simultaneously into RTs at the shared `virtualResolution`; a full-screen blend goes 0→1. Robust, works between *any* two projections (which a single-camera lerp cannot — you cannot continuously interpolate a projection matrix from perspective to orthographic without artefacts), and is independently useful for every other mode change in the game.
- **Polish pass, later: the dolly-zoom collapse.** Pull the perspective camera back while narrowing FOV; the frustum flattens and perspective converges toward orthographic. Better-looking than a dissolve when it works, but fragile and scene-specific. Do not build it first.
- `CabinetStage` already owns "apply a Cabinet to a Camera", so `CabinetTransition` is a sibling that owns "move between two of them" and hands off to `CabinetStage` at the end. It does **not** belong inside Interlude — a menu, a death, or a debug key should be able to trigger one.

There is precedent for wanting mode-to-mode continuity beyond our two features: OutBurner's shelved 2026-08-02 brainstorm states the goal as *"the game's different modes… must CONNECT visually… connective tissue is diegetic cut-scenes built from the modes' own presentation pieces, not bespoke cinematics"* (`CAMPAIGN.md:304`) and names a POV-shooter transition where *"the zoom is the perspective hand-over"* (`:314`). **Note the honest gap:** what that brainstorm actually proposes building is a *"survivor sprites"* helper — fade everything except N named sprites, glide them, fade in (`CAMPAIGN.md:316`) — a sprite-continuity trick, deliberately not a camera dissolve. So it corroborates the *goal*, not this specific component. Worth reading before finalising §4.3, since the two approaches compose well: the dissolve handles the world, the survivor sprites handle the actors that must visibly persist across it.

### 4.4 The actor hand-off: one Zoe, two views

This is the part that turns out to be nearly free, and it is the reason not to build a runtime 3D→sprite renderer.

A `Zoe` is a recipe holding stats, faction, and a **pluggable `[SerializeReference] ICharacterView view`** (`Runtime/Zoetrope/Zoe.cs:28`). `ICharacterView` is a one-method contract — `Vector2 Build(GameObject host)`, documented as *"Attach the view to `host`; return the visual's world-space size (for hurtbox sizing)"* (`Runtime/Zoetrope/ICharacterView.cs:14`). Nothing in that contract is 2D.

So: **add a `MeshView : ICharacterView` that instantiates a 3D prefab**, and the driver becomes one Zoe that can be built either way. Swapping representation at the Handover Frame is then a rebuild of the view on the same Zoe — **identity, stats, health, faction and loadout survive the genre change automatically**, because they never lived in the view. That is a much stronger position than rendering a 3D model to sprites at runtime, which would cost a whole new pipeline (§2) and buy nothing the view swap doesn't already give.

*Caveat, unverified:* no dual-representation pattern exists anywhere in the codebase today, so this is an argument from the shape of the interface, not from precedent. It should be prototyped before the phasing in §8 is committed to.

### 4.5 Scene topology: additive and co-located, never a hard load

Today the cross-genre hand-off in OutBurner is a hard cut: `MetaGame.cs:443-458` sets `SubGame.Context` then calls `SceneManager.LoadScene("Scavenge")` — non-additive, a visible seam. `INTERLUDE_DESIGN.md` §2 already flags this as *"unsolved"*.

It is solvable, and the project has already solved it once in the other direction: the road ambush deliberately does **not** change scene — `NetAmbushHost.cs:16-19`: *"An ambush happens on the road you were driving, with your car and your driver… **There is no load, no scene, no regeneration and no teleport anywhere in this file**"* — written as an explicit correction after an earlier build got it wrong by using a separate scene.

Apply the same ruling: **load the side-scroller's Cartographer level additively, offset far from the racing volume, before the car stops.** Both worlds are then live at once, each with its own camera and Cabinet, and the transition is purely a camera/authority cross-fade. Precise world offset is irrelevant (§4.1) — nothing needs to match except the screen.

The cost is a load spike, which is exactly what the sequence's front half is for: the slide turn, the door opening and the walk are **the loading screen**, diegetically. That is a well-understood technique and it is free here.

### 4.6 "Screen starts to scroll right. Platforms and buildings are revealed."

This is the part the architecture is most ready for, with one honest asterisk. `Arena` advances a view through a level's Rooms with per-Room scroll behaviour and catch-up rules, exposes `ViewCenter`, and `RoomCameraBinder` binds a Camera to it. `LevelCollision.SideScroll` is the level schema's *default* (`LevelAsset.cs:111`).

**The asterisk: nothing in this repo has ever run it.** `Arena`'s GUID appears in no scene, prefab or asset here; the demo scenes whose names suggest otherwise do not use it (`ArenaDemo` is a Choreographer/Pyre/Chunks click-demo, `ColosseumDemo` is a shmup demo with its own `ShmupDirector`). Its one real wiring anywhere is OutBurner's `ScavengeGame.cs:838`. So the correct expectation is "a designed, documented, pure-function system that needs a first proving scene here", not "a road already paved". Standing that scene up is cheap and is worth doing early, because it de-risks item 3 of §8's Track 1.

With that caveat, the run-and-gun half of the target feature is structurally a Cartographer level with side-scroll rooms driven by an Arena. **No new genre engine is required** — only the gameplay verbs. Those genuinely do not exist: OutBurner's on-foot combat is a fixed Cabal-style shooter with no platforming, no gravity and no side-view player controller.

---

## 5. Problem B — Interlude, rescoped

### 5.1 What changed since `INTERLUDE_DESIGN.md`

- **§9's blocker is real, and correctly scoped by the doc itself.** Re-verified: `ScavengeGame.cs:1630-1632` (*"reaching the door IS finishing the room… the ONLY call anywhere that ends a run successfully"*) → `Finish()` at `:1686`, and no `BeginRoom`/`TeardownRoom` exists in either repo. The doc already labels this OutBurner-side work gating *"the first real consumer"* rather than the tool, and that framing is right. **The useful addition is only this:** build Interlude against `Arena`, whose lifecycle is genre-neutral and already exposes the `RoomCleared` seam, and §9 stays a consumer problem instead of becoming a tool problem.
- **Cabinets exist and the design doc never mentions them** — the one substantive blind spot. Any conclusion it draws about backdrops, framing or the 3D hand-off was drawn without them.
- **§13's divergence still holds and is bigger than stated** — see §6.
- Minor: §13 lists `actorSortingOrder` as OutBurner-only; it is present here at `LevelAsset.cs:122`.

### 5.2 The residue really is small — but not for the reason §8 guessed

`INTERLUDE_DESIGN.md` §8 asks whether Interlude is a thin composition of Choreographer + Switcheroo + Overture. Having checked all three: **Choreographer yes** (it already drives transforms along paths), **Switcheroo yes as a 0→1 progress driver** (`Runtime/Switcheroo/Switcheroo.cs`), **Overture no** — it is a hierarchical async state machine for whole-scene/menu flow (`Runtime/Overture/OvertureState.cs:8-9`), not per-agent possession, and bending it into that role would be forcing it.

Strip out what exists and Interlude's genuinely new runtime residue is three things:

1. **The sequence document** — tracks, blocks, durations, plus the skippable-vs-consequential flag per step (`INTERLUDE_DESIGN.md` §7.2, still correct and still cheap now / expensive later).
2. **The resolver** — the string→thing lookup: named spot → position (exists, `TryGetSpot`), named group → actors (**new**), named verb → game-supplied delegate (**new**, but the pattern is `Arena.RoomCleared` widened).
3. **Possession** — see below.

Everything else is orchestration over parts that already work.

### 5.3 Possession is the real missing runtime piece

`AnimationArbiter` solves "who decides what the body is *showing*". Nothing solves "who decides where the body *is*". `TopDownMotionDriver` reads input and moves the transform with no concept of being overridden.

**Recommendation: one flag, on the driver, not a new system.** A driver that is possessed stops consuming input and stops writing the transform; Interlude drives the transform via `ChoreographyPlayer` and publishes the resulting motion through `MotionStateSource.PublishOverride` (`MotionState.cs:122`) so the animation layer sees a truthful walk instead of a slide.

*One caveat on reuse:* `PublishOverride` was written for the **opposite** case — its docstring describes faking motion *"with no real transform movement to infer it from"* (Mirage's motion preview). Using it to describe motion that IS really happening is a sound fit, but it is a new use of the method, so expect to widen or clarify it rather than to call it untouched.

This also resolves `INTERLUDE_DESIGN.md` §7.1 (transform vs animation authority, "if they disagree, feet slide"): the answer is that **the transform mover always publishes a motion state**, so they cannot disagree. That is a stronger answer than "decide per step" and it should replace it.

### 5.4 The authoring surface — and the one large build item

The two-pane shape proposed in §12 of the design doc (top = WHERE, a read-only level backdrop with paths on it; bottom = WHEN, tracks) is sound and survives everything found here. Its cost is concentrated in one place: **there is no timeline control in ZUI.** `ZuiStepSequencer` is a value painter, not a timeline. This is the biggest single item in the whole document and it should be sized honestly rather than discovered mid-build.

The sizing is not as bad as "from scratch", though: **PyrePlus CherryFraming is a working single-track slot strip** — drag-reorderable slots, each with a duration multiplier in beats (`Runtime/PyrePlus/CherryFrame.cs`, `Editor/PyrePlus/PyrePlusWindow.CherryFraming.cs`). The genuinely new work in `ZuiTrackStrip` is *multiple parallel rows sharing one time axis*, plus a playhead. Read CherryFraming's implementation before starting — it has already paid for the drag-reorder gesture bugs.

It is also the item with the most other customers already waiting — the deferred Mirage Zoe-event sequencer, SpriteFx stacks, Zoe events. If it is built once, in ZUI, as `ZuiTrackStrip`, it pays for itself several times. Per the project's ZUI-first rule this is the correct place for it regardless.

### 5.5 Procgen: the contract is already in the schema

Interlude must work over procgen levels, not just authored ones. The schema already carries both halves: **named spots** (a sequence asks for `landing-pad`, generation must guarantee it exists) and **`reservedAreas`** (`CartographerRoom.cs:113`), a rectangle generation must leave traversable. The design doc's reasoning for reserved areas over switching collision off is worth restating because it is right: collision-off still *looks* wrong the moment the hero walks through a wall the camera can see.

The obligation this creates on the generator — "a Room declaring spot X must produce spot X" — is currently written down nowhere in code. It should become a validation, not a convention.

---

## 6. The prerequisite nobody can route around: repo divergence

Measured today, both sides:

| | Laubrary Dev | OutBurner |
|---|---|---|
| `CartographerWindow.Canvas.cs` | **absent** | **2362 lines** |
| `CartographerWindow.Guides.cs` | **absent** | **995 lines** |
| `CartographerWindow.SceneTools.cs` | 557 lines (the *deleted-by-decree* path) | — |
| `ZuiPanZoom` / `ZuiPinCard` | **absent** | 265 / 191 lines |
| `ZuiChip` / `ZuiAssetHook` | **present** | absent |
| `LevelAsset.cs` | 416 | **641** |
| `Prop.cs` | 170 | **252** |

Laubrary Dev's Cartographer still declares *"The Scene view is the canvas, this file is the brush"* (`CartographerWindow.SceneTools.cs:9`) — the editing model that decree 2026-08-03 killed. **Any Interlude editor work started in this repo today would be built against a Cartographer that no longer exists in its modern form.** This is a hard prerequisite: sync first, or build in OutBurner and back-port. It is ~3400 lines of editor code plus a doubled `LevelAsset` schema moving one way, and two ZUI controls each way.

---

## 7. Does Interlude drive the 3D→2D transition?

**Yes — and the original instinct that it might not be practical was half right.**

The distinction that makes it work: **Interlude authors *time*, and it addresses things by name.** It never needs to know that the racer is 3D. A sequence saying *"car → verb `slide-to-mark`; wait; driver → verb `exit-vehicle`; driver → walk path P (spot-relative start, screen-space exit); in parallel, cabinet → transition to `SideScroller` over 1.2s; UI → splash 'STAGE 1'"* is entirely genre-agnostic. Every capitalised noun is a name the game answers.

What is **not** practical is the other half — **authoring that sequence over a 3D backdrop in a 2D level-canvas editor.** The editor's top pane is a read-only Cartographer level render; a racing scene has no cells to render. So:

> **Interlude's runtime is genre-agnostic and should drive the hand-off. Interlude's *editor* is Cartographer-strict, and the 3D half of a transition sequence gets authored as named verbs with no spatial preview.**

That is a clean, honest split, it matches the v1 scope decision already taken (Cartographer-strict), and it costs nothing structurally — exactly the argument §12 of the design doc already makes about deferred backdrops. A live-game-view backdrop can be added later if authoring the 3D half blind proves painful; the point is that it is not on the critical path.

The seam that connects them is the parked one-line change: a `RoomExit.Handoff` case meaning *"this Room ends by handing off elsewhere"* (OutBurner `TASKS.md:135`). The division of labour was already stated correctly at `INTERLUDE_DESIGN.md:53` — ***"Arena initiates · Interlude performs · SubGame transports"*** — and the only thing this document adds is what closes the visible seam that line flags: **the Cabinet transition plus the additive level.**

---

## 8. Proposed order of work

Sequenced so that each step is independently useful and nothing is blocked on a decision that hasn't been made. Sizes are rough.

**Track 1 — presentation (no Interlude dependency, start anytime)**
1. `CabinetTransition` — dual-camera RT cross-dissolve between two Cabinets. *(S–M)*
2. `MeshView : ICharacterView` + a spike proving one Zoe builds 3D or 2D from the same asset. *(S — prototype before committing to §4.4)*
3. Additive co-located level load + a throwaway hardcoded hand-off, to prove the Handover Frame reads as continuous on screen. *(M — this is the risk-retirement step for feature A, and it is worth doing before anything in Track 3)*

**Track 2 — runtime possession and Arena proving (small, unblocks everything in B)**
4. **An Arena proving scene in this repo** — a side-scroll level, rooms, `RoomCameraBinder`, played. Arena has never run here (§4.6); this retires that risk for a few hours' work and gives every later item something to test against. *(S, do it first in this track)*
5. Possession flag on `TopDownMotionDriver`; `ChoreographyPlayer` output routed through `MotionStateSource.PublishOverride`. *(S)*
6. Coordinate-space tag on the shared path type — world / spot-relative / screen. *(S)*
7. `RoomExit.Handoff` enum case, added on `CartographerRoom.cs:7-15` and handled in `Arena`'s two switches. *(XS)*

**Track 3 — Interlude proper (gated on §6)**
8. **Repo sync** — Cartographer + `ZuiPanZoom`/`ZuiPinCard` into Laubrary Dev; `ZuiChip`/`ZuiAssetHook` back. *(L, unavoidable, gates 9–13)*
9. `ZuiTrackStrip` in ZUI, starting from CherryFraming's slot strip (§5.4). *(L — the big one; several waiting customers)*
10. Extract `LevelBackdrop` (the read-only half of `LevelCanvas`). *(M)*
11. The sequence document + resolver (spot / group / verb) + skippable-vs-consequential. *(M)*
12. Path tool on the backdrop; scrub + pooled actor ghosts. *(M)*
13. Runtime player, driven off `Arena.Tick`. *(M)*

**Not on the critical path, deliberately:** platformer verbs (gravity, jumping, side-view controller) do not exist anywhere yet and are a separate gameplay-module build. Feature A's *transition* can be proven with a walking character before any platforming exists.

---

## 9. Decisions needed

Numbered so they can be answered individually; none of them block Track 1 or Track 2.

1. **Repo strategy** (§6) — sync Cartographer into Laubrary Dev *(recommended)*, or build Interlude in OutBurner and back-port? This is the one genuine gate.
2. **Handover Frame authoring** — is the screen-space mark authored per transition, or is there one global convention (e.g. "handed-over actor always lands at 40% / 60%")? Cheaper to start global.
3. **Cross-dissolve vs dolly-zoom** as the shipped look for the 3D→2D moment (§4.3). Recommend building the dissolve and treating the zoom as optional polish.
4. **Does the driver Zoe carry both views on one asset**, or are they two Zoes sharing an identity? Affects §4.4's "stats survive automatically" claim.
5. **Sequence storage** — inline on `LevelAsset` beside `rooms` *(recommended)*, or its own asset with AssetKit CRUD? Unchanged from `INTERLUDE_DESIGN.md` §13, still unanswered.
6. **Spot quick-add** — may Interlude *write* spots back to a level, or is placing a spot always a Cartographer-window trip? Making it a writer is a bigger commitment than it looks.

---

## 10. Corrections to `INTERLUDE_DESIGN.md`

Recorded so the doc is not built on twice:

- **The doc has no awareness of `Cabinets`** — the one real omission, and it is the system that owns the perspective/genre change. Everything it says about backdrops and framing should be re-read with Cabinets in mind.
- **§7.1** ("decide transform-vs-animation authority per step") should be replaced by the stronger rule in §5.3: whoever moves the transform publishes the motion state, so the two cannot disagree.
- **§13** lists `actorSortingOrder` as OutBurner-only; it exists here at `LevelAsset.cs:122`.
- **§8's composition question is now answered**: Choreographer yes, Switcheroo yes, Overture no.
- **Add a caveat to any reliance on `Arena`**: the doc is right that Arena is the systemic-time layer, but Arena has never been run in Laubrary Dev (§2/§4.6).
- **§9 stands** — recorded here because an earlier draft of this document wrongly called it obsolete. `ScavengeGame` really does end the run at the exit, and the doc already scopes that correctly as gating the first consumer rather than the tool.

---

## 11. Confidence

Every citation in this document was re-checked against the actual files by a second pass whose only job was to disprove them. That pass found and corrected nine errors in the first draft — including one that had been stated as the document's headline finding — so the confidence below is measured, not assumed.

**Verified in code** (file:line given inline): everything in §2's two tables; the OutBurner racing scene being real 3D; the hard `LoadScene` hand-off and the seamless ambush precedent; every line count in §6's divergence table; Interlude's absence from both codebases; Arena's absence from every scene in this repo.

**Reasoned, not proven** — flag before relying on: that a `MeshView` gives a clean one-Zoe-two-representations swap (§4.4 — argued from the shape of the interface; no dual-representation precedent exists anywhere in the codebase); that a dual-camera RT cross-dissolve reads as continuous at the Handover Frame (§4.2/4.3 — standard technique, never tried here); load-spike sizing for the additive level (§4.5 — unmeasured); the absence of any platforming/gravity controller in OutBurner (§4.6 — a broad negative, closed by grep over a large game file rather than by reading it end to end).

**Explicitly not assessed:** the platformer gameplay module itself; performance of two live scene volumes plus two cameras at the target virtual resolution; whether OutBurner's currently checked-out branch matches the state its design docs describe.
